stories.headline: Lula wins a fourth term in Brazil as defeated rival Flávio Bolsonaro heads to the US
stories.summary: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Brazil's Sunday runoff against far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro after trailing him in the first round. Bolsonaro's party says it recognizes the result, but he has not conceded, and President Trump called the vote 'rigged' without offering evidence. Bolsonaro missed a deadline to hand his passports to police in a money-laundering inquiry, and sources cited by Reuters and other outlets say he has left for the United States.
stories.why_it_matters: Brazilians get four more years of Lula's government, but the loser's reported departure for the US and Trump's fraud claim set up friction with Washington. Markets fell sharply on the result, and a sinking currency can push up prices in Brazil while Lula decides how to pay for his campaign promises.
stories.background: Lula, the leftist incumbent, was seeking a fourth term against Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator and son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was a close ally of Donald Trump while in office. Flávio finished first in the first round earlier this month with about 47% of valid votes to Lula's 45%, according to the official count, which forced Sunday's runoff. The Trump administration has previously alleged that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil. Flávio is under federal police investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering, and a Supreme Court judge ordered him to surrender his passports hours after his loss.

facts.text: Lula won a fourth term in Sunday's runoff, coming back after trailing Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round.
In the first round, with all polling sections counted, Flávio Bolsonaro had 47.03% of valid votes and Lula 45.16%.
Bolsonaro's party said it recognizes Lula's victory, but Flávio Bolsonaro has refused to concede.
President Trump said the election looked 'rigged'; NPR and The Hindu reported that he cited no evidence.
World leaders congratulated Lula on his reelection.
Hours after the loss, a Supreme Court ruling citing a money-laundering case barred Flávio Bolsonaro from leaving Brazil and ordered him to surrender his passports.
He missed the deadline to hand over the passports, and they were cancelled on Tuesday.
Sources and media reports say he has left Brazil for the United States, and Fox News reported that he headed to Florida; the US embassy in Brazil did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Brazil's markets and currency fell sharply on Monday after the result.
Concern about how the economy will be managed gave Brazil's currency its worst day in more than 25 years, the Financial Times reported.
The result rattled Brazilian markets and leaves Lula weighing costly campaign promises against pressure to rein in spending, CNBC reported.

stories.headline: Israelis vote in record numbers in an election seen as a verdict on Netanyahu
stories.summary: Israelis voted Tuesday in the first national election since the Hamas-led attack of Oct. 7, 2023, a contest widely described as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Turnout ran at its highest level in decades, and the Central Elections Committee turned down a request from the Likud and Shas parties to keep polls open longer. Polls close at 10 p.m. local time, and the result may not quickly settle who forms the next government.
stories.why_it_matters: The winner will lead Israel through unresolved wars in Gaza and with Iran, and NBC noted the outcome could affect the United States and gas prices.
stories.background: Netanyahu is already the longest-serving prime minister in Israel's history and is wanted by the International Criminal Court. His standing has been hurt by anger over the failure to prevent the Oct. 7 attack, wars in Gaza and with Iran, Israel's growing international isolation and the rising cost of living. He argues that only he can finish the job started in the war with Iran eight months ago, and President Trump has endorsed him. His main challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who leads the opposition bloc. After the vote, parties must bargain to form a government, which is why the count alone may not decide who leads.

facts.text: It is Israel's first national election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack and is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu.
Turnout was unusually high, with several outlets calling it the highest in decades.
Turnout reached 55.7% by 4 p.m., up 8 percentage points from the same time in 2022 and the highest ever recorded at that hour.
Four hours before polls closed, two-thirds of voters had cast ballots, the highest level since 1973, Axios reported; The Hill called it a 53-year high.
Turnout in the 1973 election was 78.6%, according to the Israel Democracy Institute.
Likud and Shas asked to extend voting hours, and the Central Elections Committee rejected the request.
Polls close at 10 p.m. local time.
Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad flew in to vote.
Netanyahu has insisted that only he can finish the job started eight months ago in Iran; a senior adviser made the same case to the New York Sun.
President Trump endorsed Netanyahu, who touted the endorsement on the eve of the vote.
Netanyahu's right-wing coalition faces an opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff; polls before the vote showed no bloc with a clear majority.
Accountability for the government's failures around the Oct. 7 attack is a central campaign issue, alongside the wars and the cost of living.

The New York Times said the vote is unlikely to yield quick answers about who will lead the next government, and the Wall Street Journal said it could be weeks or longer before a new prime minister is picked.

stories.headline: Local truce takes hold in Ukraine's Oleshky as Finland and Norway leaders call Putin
stories.summary: A local ceasefire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump took effect early Tuesday around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine, meant to let aid in and civilians out, while Russia fired missiles and drones at other Ukrainian cities. The same day, Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a rare direct call with Vladimir Putin about ending the war, drawing criticism from Denmark and Estonia.
stories.why_it_matters: The truce tests on a small scale whether Russia and Ukraine can hold a ceasefire, and the call shows Europe split over talking to Putin ahead of planned US-led peace talks that will shape the end of the war.
stories.background: Russia has occupied Oleshky, in the war-divided Kherson region, since February 2022, and residents have been cut off from food and medicine. On Oct. 23, Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators agreed to pause fighting there so aid could enter and residents could leave through a safe corridor, and the White House credited Melania Trump with securing the deal. European leaders have mostly avoided direct contact with Putin, so the Finnish and Norwegian call broke with that stance. Stubb and Støre had held a joint press conference with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo the week before.

facts.text: A local ceasefire around Oleshky took effect early Tuesday; Russia and Ukraine both said they would observe it from 3 a.m. local time.
The pause is meant to let humanitarian aid into the city and evacuate residents who want to leave.
The White House said the truce was secured by Melania Trump, who has called the situation in the city 'dire'.
Melania Trump said the ceasefire had been expanded within the Kherson region.
The White House has said 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, mostly elderly, down from about 24,000 before the war.
Residents have been cut off from food and medicine, and the BBC reported that some ate weeds to survive.
Russia launched missiles and drones at cities across Ukraine, including Kyiv, as the truce began.
The front line near Oleshky was quiet for the first time in years, with both sides halting drone attacks, the Guardian reported.
Stubb and Støre said they held a 'frank and substantive' discussion with Putin; Stubb said ending the war requires direct discussions.
Reuters called the call a rare direct contact by Europeans with Putin.
The call split European leaders over whether to engage with Putin.
Denmark's Frederiksen criticized Finland and Norway for calling Putin without coordinating with allies, though they had consulted Ukraine.
Estonia's foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, also expressed skepticism about the call in a post on X.
Kyiv said it hoped the call would bring 'new momentum' to peace talks.
Putin went on an extended tangent about Russian history during the call, the Financial Times reported.
The White House has proposed Russian deals for US oil majors as part of peace talks, in an effort to bring Putin to the table, the Financial Times reported.
Stubb, Støre and Zelenskyy held a joint press conference the week before, Norway's government said.

stories.headline: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 confirmed cases
stories.summary: Confirmed cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak rose above 10,000, government data showed Tuesday, and nearly half of those patients have died. The outbreak is driven by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment, and cases have turned up in Kenya and Nigeria.
stories.why_it_matters: With no vaccine for this strain, containment depends on finding and isolating cases, and attacks on health workers and strikes over unpaid wages make that harder. Cases in Kenya and Nigeria show how far it can travel.
stories.background: The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rarer species of Ebola that the existing approved Ebola vaccine does not target. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak in Congo and Uganda a global health emergency in May. By early October Congo had reported more than 8,400 confirmed cases across seven provinces, including Ituri and North and South Kivu, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. Cases have since been confirmed in Kenya and Nigeria.

facts.text: Confirmed Ebola cases in Congo rose above 10,000, government data showed on Tuesday.
Nearly half of the 10,060 confirmed cases have died, making it the deadliest and fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record, according to AP's report.
DW put the death toll at nearly 4,900.
As of Oct. 2, Congo had reported 8,442 confirmed cases and 4,080 deaths across seven provinces.
There is no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo virus driving the outbreak.
Health workers in Congo have been attacked and have gone on strike over unpaid wages.
Nigeria's first confirmed Ebola patient was evacuated to Switzerland.
Kenya announced its second Ebola death, a close relative of its first patient; seven other patients are being treated in isolation and no new infections were reported.
Twenty contacts of Kenya's first case were released after completing the 21-day quarantine, UN News reported.
The WHO declared the outbreak in Congo and Uganda a global health emergency.

stories.headline: Two men charged in UK over alleged Iran-backed plot at US-used air base
stories.summary: Two 24-year-old London men appeared in a London court Tuesday charged under Britain's National Security Act over a September incident at RAF Fairford, an English air base used by US bombers in the war against Iran. Prosecutors described it as an Iran-backed plot against the base, and one of the men is charged with helping Iranian intelligence, according to the New York Times. The court was told the men were directed by a handler whom police believe was working for Iran.
stories.why_it_matters: British authorities allege that Iran backed a plot against a base on British soil used by US forces in the war, a sign that the conflict's risks reach allies that host those forces.
stories.background: RAF Fairford is a base in England used by the US military, including bombers in its war against Iran. In September there was an incident at the base that British authorities have blamed on Iran. Counter-terrorism police arrested and later re-arrested suspects on suspicion of assisting Iranian intelligence, an offense under the National Security Act passed in 2023. On Tuesday prosecutors charged two men and they appeared in court in London.

facts.text: Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim, a British-Iranian dual national, and Nouman Essghir, a British citizen, both 24 and from London, were charged under the National Security Act.
The two appeared in a London court on Tuesday.
Prosecutors say the incident was an Iran-backed plot against the US-run base, and the UK has blamed the incident on Iran.
One man is charged with helping Iranian intelligence, the New York Times reported; authorities say one suspect is linked to Iran.
A court was told that a handler known as Ali, whom police believe was working on behalf of Iran, directed a group of men to drive vans loaded with petrol to the base, the Guardian reported.
The incident happened in September at RAF Fairford, a key base for US bombers used in the war against Iran.
On Oct. 20, counter-terrorism police re-arrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iran over the Fairford incident.

stories.headline: Jordan strikes militants in Syria after church attack; Syria says civilians were killed
stories.summary: Jordan's air force struck what it called Islamic State hideouts in southern Syria late Monday, saying the groups were linked to last week's deadly attack on a church in Jordan. Jordan said it killed more than 20 militants and expressed regret for civilian casualties, while Syria condemned the strikes as an 'unacceptable violation'.
stories.why_it_matters: The strikes have opened the worst rift between the two neighbors since Bashar al-Assad fell, and show how a single attack can spill across a border.
stories.background: On Oct. 23, gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan, and the death toll rose to nine. Jordan says the attackers were linked to militant groups in southern Syria, which it identifies as Islamic State. Jordan's air force has struck Islamic State targets in Syria before, joining US strikes in December 2025. Syria has had a new government since longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad was ousted in December 2024.

stories.headline: India evacuates tens of thousands as Cyclone Arnab nears Andhra Pradesh
stories.summary: Indian authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people from coastal Andhra Pradesh ahead of Cyclone Arnab, which is forecast to make landfall Wednesday as a very severe cyclone with winds of 125-135 km/h and then head inland toward Nepal. Trains and flights were cancelled, and heavy rain had already brought Visakhapatnam to a standstill.
stories.why_it_matters: People along India's east coast face flooding, wind damage and travel disruption, and a track inland toward Nepal could carry heavy rain well beyond the coast.
stories.background: Arnab formed over the Bay of Bengal and has been strengthening as it approaches India's east coast. Andhra Pradesh and neighboring Odisha have stepped up preparations, and Odisha's government set a goal of zero casualties. Authorities have opened cyclone shelters across vulnerable districts and suspended some transport.

facts.text: Authorities evacuated tens of thousands of people from vulnerable coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh.
Arnab is forecast to intensify into a very severe cyclone and make landfall on the Andhra Pradesh coast on Wednesday, Oct. 28, with winds of 125-135 km/h.
Gusts could reach 150 km/h as the storm crosses the coast.
After landfall the storm is expected to cut inland and head north toward Nepal.
Train services and flights were cancelled and cyclone shelters activated; India's Civil Aviation Ministry reviewed flight safety.
Heavy rain brought Visakhapatnam to a standstill, with 147.9 mm falling between 8:30 a.m. and 9 p.m., and bus services were cancelled.
Odisha's government set a target of zero casualties as it prepared for the storm.

stories.headline: Machado returns to Venezuela; Rubio says the interim government agreed to let her in
stories.summary: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, last year's Nobel Peace Prize winner, made a surprise return to Venezuela after nearly a year in exile and was greeted by large crowds. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Venezuela's interim government told the US weeks earlier that she could return without interference, though he also warned, without naming her, against trying to 'street-protest' into democracy. The Nobel committee and congressional Democrats are pressing for elections.
stories.why_it_matters: Her return tests whether Venezuela's US-backed interim government will allow open opposition politics and move toward new elections, decisions in which Washington now has a large say.
stories.background: In January, Nicolás Maduro was captured in a US military operation, and Delcy Rodríguez took over as acting president at the head of an interim government. Machado, who won the Nobel Peace Prize last year, had said for months that she would return. The Trump administration has worked with the existing interim leadership, and Machado wants new elections and a change of government.

facts.text: Machado made a surprise return to Venezuela, where she was greeted by large crowds, NBC reported.

Without naming Machado, Rubio told reporters on Monday, 'You're not going to street-protest your way into a democracy.'
The Norwegian Nobel Committee, which gave Machado last year's Peace Prize, said Venezuela still needs democratic change.
Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and other Democrats urged Venezuela's government to hold elections.
Machado wants to revive her movement and persuade Washington that Venezuela needs a change of government, the Wall Street Journal reported.
The BBC said Washington appears content with Venezuela's existing leader for now, and the New York Times said Machado must avoid offending the Trump administration while asserting her own leadership.
